1.label: Category 1 — Psychological Dominant
1.verdict: Your symptoms are primarily psychological — things like mood swings, foggy thinking, and anxiety. These are common early signs of hormonal imbalance in women.
1.body: Psychological symptoms such as mood swings, irritability, foggy thinking, and low libido are frequently linked to fluctuating estrogen and progesterone levels, along with disrupted cortisol patterns. These shifts affect neurotransmitter activity and can significantly impact mood, focus, and energy well before more obvious physical symptoms appear. A hormone panel covering estrogen, progesterone, and cortisol can help clarify what is driving these symptoms.

steps.title: Get a full hormone panel
steps.body: Estrogen, progesterone, and cortisol levels will show whether hormonal imbalance is contributing to your psychological symptoms.

steps.title: Prioritize sleep and stress management
steps.body: Poor sleep and chronic stress both disrupt hormone production and worsen mood-related symptoms.

steps.title: Speak to a specialist
steps.body: A personalized consultation can help you understand whether hormone therapy is appropriate for you.

2.label: Category 2 — Reproductive & Hormonal Dominant
2.verdict: Your symptoms are primarily reproductive and hormonal — this pattern is classically associated with estrogen and androgen imbalance in women.
2.body: Symptoms like menstrual irregularities, heavy menses, acne, and increased body/facial hair are among the most recognized signs of a reproductive hormone imbalance, such as excess androgens or estrogen dominance. These symptoms often develop gradually and are frequently dismissed, when in fact they are treatable with the right diagnosis and care.

steps.title: Test your reproductive hormone levels
steps.body: A panel covering estrogen, testosterone, and androgens is the standard first step in diagnosing a reproductive hormone imbalance.

steps.title: Ask about a pelvic ultrasound
steps.body: If symptoms like cystic ovaries or fibroids are present, imaging can help identify underlying structural causes.

steps.title: Book a free consultation
steps.body: Our specialists can walk you through treatment options based on your specific hormone pattern.

3.label: Category 3 — Metabolic & Physical Dominant
3.verdict: Your symptoms point to metabolic and physical changes — fatigue, weight gain, and low activity are common when hormone and thyroid function decline together.
3.body: Metabolic symptoms such as persistent fatigue, difficulty losing weight, and hot flashes often reflect a combination of declining hormone levels and slowing metabolism. Left unaddressed, this pattern can progress and make daily life increasingly difficult, making early evaluation valuable.

steps.title: Check hormone and thyroid levels together
steps.body: Hormonal imbalance and thyroid dysfunction often overlap and worsen each other — both should be tested.

steps.title: Get a metabolic panel
steps.body: Fasting glucose, HbA1c, and a lipid panel will show whether metabolic markers need attention.

steps.title: Combine movement with treatment
steps.body: Regular physical activity helps manage weight and energy, and works well alongside any hormone therapy you pursue.

4.label: Category 4 — Cardiovascular & Chronic Disease Risk Dominant
4.verdict: Your symptoms point mainly toward cardiovascular and chronic disease risk factors, which are closely linked to hormonal health in women.
4.body: Elevated cholesterol, blood pressure, blood sugar, or a personal/family history of heart disease and diabetes are all connected to hormone levels — hormonal decline is associated with increased cardiovascular risk, and treating it appropriately (alongside standard care) is an important part of a complete picture.

steps.title: Get a cardiometabolic workup
steps.body: Lipid panel, blood pressure, fasting glucose/HbA1c, and a hormone panel should all be assessed together.

steps.title: Talk to your doctor about your family history
steps.body: Family history of heart disease or diabetes changes how aggressively these risk factors should be managed.

steps.title: Ask about hormone-related cardiovascular risk
steps.body: Our specialists can help you understand how hormone levels interact with your cardiovascular risk profile.

5.label: Category 5 — Multiple Systems Affected
5.verdict: You are experiencing symptoms across all four areas — psychological, reproductive, metabolic, and cardiovascular. This broad pattern is common with significant hormonal imbalance and deserves a comprehensive evaluation.
5.body: When symptoms span psychological, reproductive, metabolic, and cardiovascular categories simultaneously, it usually indicates that hormonal decline has been affecting your body for some time across multiple systems. This is a common pattern seen in women with clinically significant hormone imbalance, and it typically responds well to a structured, comprehensive treatment plan.

steps.title: Get a comprehensive hormone & metabolic panel
steps.body: Estrogen, progesterone, androgens, thyroid, lipids, blood sugar, and cortisol together will give a complete picture of what is driving your symptoms.

steps.title: Speak with a specialist as soon as possible
steps.body: With symptoms across every category, a personalized treatment plan — rather than addressing symptoms individually — will likely be most effective.

steps.title: Start with lifestyle foundations
steps.body: Sleep, movement, and nutrition support any hormone therapy you and your specialist decide to pursue.

1.verdict: Your symptoms are primarily psychological and cognitive — things like mood changes, low motivation, and mental fog. These are common early signs of hormonal imbalance in men.
1.body: Psychological symptoms such as irritability, apathy, brain fog, and low libido are frequently linked to declining testosterone and disrupted cortisol patterns. These changes affect neurotransmitter activity and can significantly impact mood, focus, and drive well before more obvious physical symptoms appear. A hormone panel that includes total and free testosterone, along with cortisol, can clarify what is driving these symptoms.

steps.title: Get a full hormone panel
steps.body: Total & free testosterone, SHBG, and cortisol will show whether hormonal imbalance is contributing to your psychological symptoms.

steps.title: Prioritize sleep and stress management
steps.body: Poor sleep and chronic stress both suppress testosterone production and worsen mood-related symptoms.

steps.title: Speak to a specialist
steps.body: A personalized consultation can help you understand whether hormone optimization therapy is appropriate for you.

2.label: Category 2 — Sexual & Urinary Dominant
2.verdict: Your symptoms are primarily sexual and urinary in nature — this pattern is classically associated with low testosterone (Low-T) in men.
2.body: Symptoms like decreased erections, erectile dysfunction, reduced stamina, and urinary changes are among the most recognized signs of testosterone deficiency. These symptoms often develop gradually and are frequently dismissed as a normal part of aging, when in fact they are treatable with the right diagnosis and care.

steps.title: Test your testosterone levels
steps.body: A morning blood draw for total and free testosterone is the standard first step in diagnosing Low-T.

steps.title: Rule out prostate issues
steps.body: A PSA test and prostate exam help rule out other causes of urinary symptoms before starting any treatment.

steps.title: Book a free consultation
steps.body: Our specialists can walk you through treatment options, including testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), if appropriate.

3.label: Category 3 — Metabolic & Physical Dominant
3.verdict: Your symptoms point to metabolic and physical changes — weight gain, muscle loss, and low activity are common when testosterone and thyroid function decline together.
3.body: Metabolic symptoms such as increasing waist size, difficulty losing weight, and decreased muscle mass often reflect a combination of declining testosterone and slowing metabolism. Left unaddressed, this pattern can progress toward metabolic syndrome, making early evaluation valuable.

steps.title: Check testosterone and thyroid together
steps.body: Low testosterone and thyroid dysfunction often overlap and worsen each other — both should be tested.

steps.title: Get a metabolic panel
steps.body: Fasting glucose, HbA1c, and a lipid panel will show whether metabolic syndrome markers are present.

steps.title: Combine strength training with treatment
steps.body: Resistance training helps preserve muscle mass and works synergistically with any hormone therapy you pursue.

4.body: Elevated cholesterol, blood pressure, blood sugar, or a personal/family history of heart disease and diabetes are all connected to testosterone levels — low testosterone is associated with increased cardiovascular risk, and treating it appropriately (alongside standard cardiac care) is an important part of a complete picture.
